# Research sources

<!-- Generated by scripts/skill_library.py from data/research.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

Each citation (authors, year, title, venue) was confirmed to exist by web search on the check date. Volume and page numbers are omitted because they were not confirmed. Findings are summarised from prior knowledge of each source; no full text was re-read on the check date, so read the source before relying on a specific number.

Weight says how much a source can bear when deciding what a caregiver does at home with a child of 4-6: `strong`, `moderate` or `weak`. It is this project's judgement, not a rating taken from the source. For the synthesis by area, read [research-base.md](research-base.md).

## Cross-cutting

### `bailey-2020`

Bailey, D. H., Duncan, G. J., Cunha, F., Foorman, B. R., & Yeager, D. S. (2020). Persistence and fade-out of educational-intervention effects: Mechanisms and potential solutions. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7787577/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 0 mo to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Effects of early interventions on the skills they target usually shrink after the intervention ends. Persistence is more likely when later environments keep building on the skill, or when the intervention changes something that would not have developed anyway.
- Limits: A review of mechanisms, and the explanation for fade-out is still debated. It concerns programs, not a parent's sustained routine.

### `alfieri-2011`

Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. [Link](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ933606)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 4 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 164 studies, unassisted discovery produced worse learning than explicit instruction, while guided discovery with feedback, worked examples or prompts produced better learning than other methods.
- Limits: Most studies involved older children and adults, not preschoolers.
- Also informs: science.

### `weisberg-2016`

Weisberg, D. S., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Golinkoff, R. M., Kittredge, A. K., & Klahr, D. (2016). Guided play: Principles and practices. Current Directions in Psychological Science. [Link](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0963721416645512)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Guided play keeps the child in control of the action while an adult chooses the materials and steers attention toward a learning goal with questions and hints.
- Limits: A short position review by proponents of the approach.
- Also informs: science, building.

### `skene-2022`

Skene, K., O'Farrelly, C. M., Byrne, E. M., Kirby, N., Stevens, E. C., & Ramchandani, P. G. (2022). Can guidance during play enhance children's learning and development in educational contexts? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35018635/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 12 mo to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Compared with direct instruction, guided play gave better results for early maths, shape knowledge and task switching. Compared with free play, it gave better spatial vocabulary.
- Limits: 39 studies with few per outcome, mostly in classrooms. Direct instruction was not worse on most outcomes.
- Also informs: math, building, science.

### `lillard-2013`

Lillard, A. S., Lerner, M. D., Hopkins, E. J., Dore, R. A., Smith, E. D., & Palmquist, C. M. (2013). The impact of pretend play on children's development: A review of the evidence. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22905949/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 8 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Existing evidence does not support strong causal claims that pretend play drives creativity, intelligence, problem solving, theory of mind or self-regulation. It may be one of several routes to those outcomes, or a by-product.
- Limits: The conclusion is about the weakness of the evidence, not proof that pretend play does nothing.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `romeo-2018`

Romeo, R. R., Leonard, J. A., Robinson, S. T., West, M. R., Mackey, A. P., Rowe, M. L., & Gabrieli, J. D. E. (2018). Beyond the 30-million-word gap: Children's conversational exposure is associated with language-related brain function. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5945324)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y 11 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In 36 children aged 4-6, the number of adult-child conversational turns, not the number of adult words heard, was related to verbal scores and to activation in language areas, independent of family income and education.
- Limits: Small and correlational. Talkative children may draw more turns from adults.
- Also informs: reading.

## Reading

### `nelp-2008`

National Early Literacy Panel. (2008). Developing early literacy: Report of the National Early Literacy Panel. National Institute for Literacy. [Link](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/publications/pubs/Documents/NELPReport09.pdf)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 0 mo to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across roughly 300 studies, the strongest preschool predictors of later decoding, spelling and comprehension were alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, rapid naming, writing or name writing, and phonological memory. Code-focused teaching improved those skills. Shared reading mainly improved oral language.
- Limits: The predictors are correlational. Most intervention studies were short and school based.
- Also informs: writing.

### `castles-2018`

Castles, A., Rastle, K., & Nation, K. (2018). Ending the reading wars: Reading acquisition from novice to expert. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. [Link](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/ending-the-reading-wars-reading-acquisition-from-novice-to-expert.html)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 4 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Systematic phonics is necessary for learning to decode an alphabetic script but is not sufficient. Fluent word reading also needs a large amount of reading experience, and comprehension depends on vocabulary and knowledge of the world.
- Limits: A narrative review, mostly about school instruction.

### `ies-foundational-2016`

Foorman, B., Beyler, N., Borradaile, K., Coyne, M., Denton, C. A., Dimino, J., et al. (2016). Foundational skills to support reading for understanding in kindergarten through 3rd grade (NCEE 2016-4008). What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/21)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 5 y to 8 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Four recommendations: teach academic language (minimal evidence), teach awareness of speech sounds and letter-sound links (strong), teach decoding and word analysis (strong), and have children read connected text every day for accuracy, fluency and comprehension (moderate).
- Limits: Written for kindergarten to grade 3 classrooms. A younger child who already decodes is outside the studied population by age, though not by skill.

### `share-1995`

Share, D. L. (1995). Phonological recoding and self-teaching: Sine qua non of reading acquisition. Cognition. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7789090/)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 5 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Self-teaching hypothesis: each time a child successfully sounds out a new word, that is a learning trial that builds the word-specific memory needed for fluent reading. Decoding skill plus reading volume drives growth.
- Limits: A theoretical review. Later experiments support it, but it does not prescribe a home routine.

### `ehri-2014`

Ehri, L. C. (2014). Orthographic mapping in the acquisition of sight word reading, spelling memory, and vocabulary learning. Scientific Studies of Reading. [Link](https://www.readingrockets.org/research-by-topic/orthographic-mapping-acquisition-sight-word-reading-spelling-memory-and-vocabulary)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 4 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Words become readable at sight when their spellings are bonded to their pronunciations and meanings. That bonding needs phonemic awareness and letter-sound knowledge, and spelling and reading draw on the same knowledge.
- Limits: A theory paper summarising the author's research program.
- Also informs: writing.

### `mol-2008`

Mol, S. E., Bus, A. G., de Jong, M. T., & Smeets, D. J. H. (2008). Added value of dialogic parent-child book readings: A meta-analysis. Early Education and Development. [Link](https://www.scinapse.io/papers/2088476022)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 2 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 16 studies, training parents in dialogic reading improved children's expressive vocabulary more than ordinary reading aloud. The effect was clearly smaller for 4-5-year-olds than for 2-3-year-olds, and smaller for children at risk.
- Limits: Short-term vocabulary outcomes. For a child near 5, the gain from questioning style alone is modest.

### `senechal-2002`

Senechal, M., & LeFevre, J.-A. (2002). Parental involvement in the development of children's reading skill: A five-year longitudinal study. Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11949902)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 8 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 168 children followed from kindergarten to grade 3, storybook exposure predicted vocabulary and listening comprehension, which predicted grade 3 reading. Parents teaching letters and words predicted early literacy skills and grade 1 reading. The two paths were largely separate.
- Limits: Correlational, in middle-class Canadian families.

### `wwc-prek-2022`

What Works Clearinghouse. (2022). Preparing young children for school (WWC 2022009). Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/practiceguide/30)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Seven recommendations for preschool programs covering social-emotional skills, executive function, mathematical ideas and math talk, letters and sounds, shared book reading and vocabulary.
- Limits: The recommendation list is summarised from memory and was not re-read on the check date. Evidence levels differ by recommendation. Classroom setting.
- Also informs: math, social-emotional.

## Writing

### `ouellette-2017`

Ouellette, G., & Senechal, M. (2017). Invented spelling in kindergarten as a predictor of reading and spelling in Grade 1: A new pathway to literacy, or just the same road, less known? Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://www.readingrockets.org/research-by-topic/invented-spelling-kindergarten-predictor-reading-and-spelling-grade-1)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 7 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 170 kindergartners, how sophisticated a child's invented spellings were predicted grade 1 reading and spelling over and above phonological awareness and letter knowledge.
- Limits: Longitudinal, not experimental. The authors' separate training studies are not reviewed here.
- Also informs: reading.

### `ies-writers-2012`

Graham, S., Bollinger, A., Booth Olson, C., D'Aoust, C., MacArthur, C., McCutchen, D., & Olinghouse, N. (2012). Teaching elementary school students to be effective writers (NCEE 2012-4058). What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/17)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 5 y to 11 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Provide daily time to write (minimal evidence). Teach the writing process and writing for different purposes (strong). Teach handwriting, spelling, sentence construction and typing until fluent (moderate). Build a community of writers (minimal).
- Limits: Elementary classrooms. Preschool is out of scope.

### `santangelo-2016`

Santangelo, T., & Graham, S. (2016). A comprehensive meta-analysis of handwriting instruction. Educational Psychology Review. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9335-1)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 5 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Explicit handwriting instruction improved legibility and fluency, and also improved the quality and length of what students wrote.
- Limits: School-age samples, starting at kindergarten.

### `puranik-2011`

Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2011). From scribbles to scrabble: Preschool children's developing knowledge of written language. Reading and Writing. [Link](https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 372 preschoolers, writing knowledge developed in a consistent order: general features of writing first, then letters and name writing, then spelling. Name writing was the most advanced skill at each age.
- Limits: Descriptive. It shows a typical order, not what teaching changes.

### `grissmer-2010`

Grissmer, D., Grimm, K. J., Aiyer, S. M., Murrah, W. M., & Steele, J. S. (2010). Fine motor skills and early comprehension of the world: Two new school readiness indicators. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20822219/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 11 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Across three large longitudinal datasets, fine motor skill and general knowledge at kindergarten entry predicted later math and reading over and above early math, reading and attention.
- Limits: Correlational. It does not show that training fine motor skill raises achievement.
- Also informs: art, cross-cutting.

## Math

### `duncan-2007`

Duncan, G. J., Dowsett, C. J., Claessens, A., Magnuson, K., Huston, A. C., Klebanov, P., et al. (2007). School readiness and later achievement. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18020822/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y 6 mo to 14 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across six longitudinal datasets, math skill at school entry was the strongest predictor of later achievement, followed by reading and attention. Social-emotional behaviour at entry did not predict later achievement.
- Limits: Correlational with extensive controls. The causal effect of boosting early math is likely smaller than the correlation (see bailey-2020).
- Also informs: reading, cross-cutting.

### `siegler-2008`

Siegler, R. S., & Ramani, G. B. (2008). Playing linear numerical board games promotes low-income children's numerical development. Developmental Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18801120/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Low-income preschoolers who played a linear 1-10 number board game for four sessions of 15-20 minutes improved their number-line estimates. The same game played with colours instead of numbers did not help.
- Limits: Head Start samples. A child with strong number knowledge may already be at ceiling on a 1-10 board.

### `ramani-2008`

Ramani, G. B., & Siegler, R. S. (2008). Promoting broad and stable improvements in low-income children's numerical knowledge through playing number board games. Child Development. [Link](https://drum.lib.umd.edu/handle/1903/10061)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Replicated the board-game effect on four tasks: number-line estimation, magnitude comparison, counting and numeral identification. Gains were still present nine weeks later. Children's reported board-game play at home was related to their number knowledge.
- Limits: Head Start samples and a short follow-up.

### `ies-math-2013`

Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children (NCEE 2014-4005). What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/18)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Teach number and operations along a developmental progression (moderate evidence). Teach geometry, patterns, measurement and data (minimal). Monitor progress (minimal). Teach children to describe their world mathematically (minimal). Give math dedicated time each day and weave it through the day (minimal).
- Limits: Classroom guide for ages 3-6. Only the first recommendation has more than minimal evidence.
- Also informs: building.

### `berkowitz-2015`

Berkowitz, T., Schaeffer, M. W., Maloney, E. A., Peterson, L., Gregor, C., Levine, S. C., & Beilock, S. L. (2015). Math at home adds up to achievement in school. Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26450209/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 7 y 6 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 587 first-graders, families given an app of short math story problems to do together saw more math growth across the school year than families given a reading app, most of all when the parents were anxious about math.
- Limits: First grade, not preschool. A published comment questioned the analysis; it appeared in search results and was not reviewed.

### `levine-2010`

Levine, S. C., Suriyakham, L. W., Rowe, M. L., Huttenlocher, J., & Gunderson, E. A. (2010). What counts in the development of young children's number knowledge? Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2998540)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 mo to 3 y 10 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: The amount of number talk parents used between 14 and 30 months predicted children's understanding of cardinal number at 46 months, controlling for socioeconomic status and other talk.
- Limits: 44 families, correlational, toddler years.

### `clements-2011`

Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2011). Early childhood mathematics intervention. Science. [Link](https://researchconnect.buffalo.edu/en/publications/early-childhood-mathematics-intervention/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschool math programs built on learning trajectories raise math achievement, including for low-income children. Early math is broader than counting and includes space, shape and pattern.
- Limits: A review written by the developers of one such curriculum.
- Also informs: building.

## Science

### `bonawitz-2011`

Bonawitz, E., Shafto, P., Gweon, H., Goodman, N. D., Spelke, E., & Schulz, L. (2011). The double-edged sword of pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery. Cognition. [Link](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/60992)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschoolers who were shown one function of a new toy by a teacher explored it less and found fewer of its other functions than children who were not directly taught.
- Limits: One toy, one session, a museum sample. It shows a cost of demonstration for exploration, not that instruction is harmful in general.

### `gopnik-2012`

Gopnik, A. (2012). Scientific thinking in young children: Theoretical advances, empirical research, and policy implications. Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3422420)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschoolers test hypotheses, learn from patterns in data and from their own interventions, and infer causes in ways that resemble scientific reasoning. Exploratory play serves this.
- Limits: A review of lab studies by a leading proponent. It does not test home activities.

### `chouinard-2007`

Chouinard, M. M. (2007). Children's questions: A mechanism for cognitive development. Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17394580/)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 12 mo to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschoolers ask adults a very large number of information-seeking questions, usually get informative answers, and keep asking when they do not. With age the questions shift from facts toward explanations.
- Limits: Observational: a small number of recorded children plus diary studies.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

## Art

### `winner-2013`

Winner, E., Goldstein, T. R., & Vincent-Lancrin, S. (2013). Art for art's sake? The impact of arts education. OECD Publishing. [Link](https://www.brookings.edu/books/art-for-arts-sake-the-impact-of-arts-education/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: There is little rigorous evidence that arts education improves achievement in other school subjects. A few specific links hold up better, such as music with phonological skills and classroom drama with verbal skills. The authors conclude the arts are justified by what they teach in themselves.
- Limits: Mostly school-age samples and many weak studies.
- Also informs: music.

## Music

### `sala-2020`

Sala, G., & Gobet, F. (2020). Cognitive and academic benefits of music training with children: A multilevel meta-analysis. Memory & Cognition. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32728850/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 16 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 54 studies, music training showed a small overall effect on cognitive and academic outcomes that fell to about zero in studies with random assignment and active control groups.
- Limits: It addresses transfer to other skills, not the value of learning music.

### `schellenberg-2004`

Schellenberg, E. G. (2004). Music lessons enhance IQ. Psychological Science. [Link](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.0956-7976.2004.00711.x/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 7 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: 144 six-year-olds were randomly assigned to 36 weeks of keyboard lessons, voice lessons, drama lessons or no lessons. The music groups gained a few more IQ points than the comparison groups.
- Limits: A single study with a small effect that later meta-analysis does not support (see sala-2020).

### `kirschner-2010`

Kirschner, S., & Tomasello, M. (2010). Joint music making promotes prosocial behavior in 4-year-old children. Evolution and Human Behavior. [Link](https://www.eva.mpg.de/documents/Elsevier/Kirschner_Joint_EvolHumBeh_2010_1552719.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Pairs of four-year-olds who sang, danced and played instruments together in a game were more likely to help and cooperate with each other straight afterwards than pairs who played the same game without music.
- Limits: One lab study of 96 children measuring immediate behaviour. A later controlled field experiment appeared in search results reporting no effect; only its title was seen.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `woodruff-2014`

Woodruff Carr, K., White-Schwoch, T., Tierney, A. T., Strait, D. L., & Kraus, N. (2014). Beat synchronization predicts neural speech encoding and reading readiness in preschoolers. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25246562/)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 3 y to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Among 35 preschoolers, those who could drum in time with a beat had better pre-reading skills and more precise neural encoding of speech sounds.
- Limits: Small and correlational. It does not show that rhythm practice improves reading.
- Also informs: reading.

## Movement and sports

### `who-2019`

World Health Organization. (2019). Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age. [Link](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241550536)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 0 mo to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children aged 3-4 should get at least 180 minutes of physical activity a day, including at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity, no more than one hour of sedentary screen time, and 10-13 hours of good-quality sleep.
- Limits: WHO rates the underlying evidence as low or very low quality. The guideline stops at age 4.

### `us-pag-2018`

U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. (2018). Physical activity guidelines for Americans (2nd ed.). [Link](https://health.gov/sites/default/files/2019-10/PAG_ExecutiveSummary.pdf)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 3 y to 17 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children aged 3-5 should be physically active throughout the day. From age 6, children need at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activity.
- Limits: A guideline, with the preschool recommendation resting on thinner evidence than the school-age one.

### `logan-2012`

Logan, S. W., Robinson, L. E., Wilson, A. E., & Lucas, W. A. (2012). Getting the fundamentals of movement: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of motor skill interventions in children. Child: Care, Health and Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21880055/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 10 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Planned motor skill instruction improved children's fundamental movement skills (running, jumping, throwing, catching, kicking). Comparison groups who only had free play did not improve.
- Limits: Eleven studies, many with children who had delays or were from low-income families, and short-term outcomes.

### `stodden-2008`

Stodden, D. F., Goodway, J. D., Langendorfer, S. J., Roberton, M. A., Rudisill, M. E., Garcia, C., & Garcia, L. E. (2008). A developmental perspective on the role of motor skill competence in physical activity: An emergent relationship. Quest. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1080/00336297.2008.10483582)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Proposes that motor skill competence in early childhood drives later physical activity, perceived competence and fitness, and that the link strengthens with age. Children who lack the basic skills drop out of active play and sport.
- Limits: A conceptual model. See robinson-2015 for the supporting evidence.

### `robinson-2015`

Robinson, L. E., Stodden, D. F., Barnett, L. M., Lopes, V. P., Logan, S. W., Rodrigues, L. P., & D'Hondt, E. (2015). Motor competence and its effect on positive developmental trajectories of health. Sports Medicine. [Link](https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s40279-015-0351-6)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Reviews evidence that motor competence is positively related to physical activity, fitness and perceived competence, and inversely related to weight status, across childhood.
- Limits: Mostly correlational and cross-sectional studies.

### `aap-sports-2019`

Logan, K., Cuff, S., & Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness. (2019). Organized sports for children, preadolescents, and adolescents. Pediatrics. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31110166/)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Organized sport has physical, social and psychological benefits when it stays fun and matches the child's development. Before children are developmentally ready, free play and basic skills matter more than competition. Fun is the main reason children keep playing.
- Limits: A clinical report based on expert review. The report places readiness for organized sport at about age 6 for most children; that figure is recalled from memory and should be confirmed in the report.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `aap-specialization-2016`

Brenner, J. S., & Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness. (2016). Sports specialization and intensive training in young athletes. Pediatrics. [Link](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/138/3/e20162148/52612/Sports-Specialization-and-Intensive-Training-in)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 5 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Playing several sports and delaying single-sport specialization until late adolescence (about 15-16 for most sports) is associated with fewer injuries and less stress and burnout, and does not reduce the chance of athletic success.
- Limits: Based largely on observational studies of older athletes.

### `brussoni-2015`

Brussoni, M., Gibbons, R., Gray, C., Ishikawa, T., Sandseter, E. B. H., Bienenstock, A., et al. (2015). What is the relationship between risky outdoor play and health in children? A systematic review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483710)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 21 papers, risky outdoor play (heights, speed, rough-and-tumble, playing out of sight) was associated with more physical activity and better social health. Play at height was not associated with more or worse fractures.
- Limits: Evidence quality rated low to moderate, mostly observational.
- Also informs: nature, social-emotional.

### `brenner-2009`

Brenner, R. A., Taneja, G. S., Haynie, D. L., Trumble, A. C., Qian, C., Klinger, R. M., & Klebanoff, M. A. (2009). Association between swimming lessons and drowning in childhood: A case-control study. Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19255386)

- Design: case-control. Ages studied: 12 mo to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Formal swimming lessons were associated with an 88% lower risk of drowning in children aged 1-4 (odds ratio 0.12, 95% confidence interval 0.01 to 0.97).
- Limits: Case-control design with a very wide confidence interval. Lessons do not make a child drown-proof.

### `aap-drowning-2019`

Denny, S. A., Quan, L., Gilchrist, J., McCallin, T., Shenoi, R., Yusuf, S., et al. (2019). Prevention of drowning. Pediatrics. [Link](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/143/5/e20190850/37134/Prevention-of-Drowning)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 12 mo to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Recommends swim lessons for most children from about age 1 as one layer of protection alongside close supervision, pool barriers and life jackets.
- Limits: Newer AAP drowning statements (2021 and 2026) appeared in search results and were not reviewed.

## Social-emotional skills

### `jones-2015`

Jones, D. E., Greenberg, M., & Crowley, M. (2015). Early social-emotional functioning and public health: The relationship between kindergarten social competence and future wellness. American Journal of Public Health. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4605168)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 25 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 753 kindergartners, teacher-rated prosocial skill predicted education, employment, crime, substance use and mental health 13-19 years later, controlling for family and child characteristics.
- Limits: Correlational, in a sample weighted toward higher-risk children.

### `moffitt-2011`

Moffitt, T. E., Arseneault, L., Belsky, D., Dickson, N., Hancox, R. J., Harrington, H., et al. (2011). A gradient of childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3041102)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 3 y to 32 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 1,000 children followed to age 32, childhood self-control predicted adult health, finances and criminal offending along a gradient, controlling for intelligence and social class.
- Limits: Observational. It does not show that training self-control changes those outcomes.

### `watts-2018`

Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., & Quan, H. (2018). Revisiting the marshmallow test: A conceptual replication investigating links between early delay of gratification and later outcomes. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7197218)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y 6 mo to 15 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In a larger and more diverse sample, the link between delay of gratification at 54 months and achievement at 15 was half the size originally reported, and shrank by about two thirds once family background and early cognitive ability were controlled.
- Limits: A replication of a correlation. It cautions against treating one self-control task as a lever.

### `diamond-2011`

Diamond, A., & Lee, K. (2011). Interventions shown to aid executive function development in children 4 to 12 years old. Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3159917/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 4 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Computerized training, aerobic exercise, martial arts, mindfulness and some school curricula improved executive function. Children with the weakest executive function gained most, gains needed the challenge to keep rising, and transfer was narrow.
- Limits: A narrative review. Several of the headline programs have had mixed results since.
- Also informs: movement.

### `leonard-2021`

Leonard, J. A., Martinez, D. N., Dashineau, S. C., Park, A. T., & Mackey, A. P. (2021). Children persist less when adults take over. Child Development. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13492)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Parents who took over more during a hard puzzle had 4-5-year-olds rated as less persistent. In an experiment, children persisted less on a later task after an adult took over than after an adult taught them or did nothing.
- Limits: Short lab tasks and immediate effects.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `gunderson-2013`

Gunderson, E. A., Gripshover, S. J., Romero, C., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2013). Parent praise to 1- to 3-year-olds predicts children's motivational frameworks 5 years later. Child Development. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3655123)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 mo to 8 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: The share of parents' praise that was about effort and strategy when children were 14-38 months old predicted the children's belief, at age 7-8, that ability can grow.
- Limits: 53 families, correlational. See sisk-2018 for how small mindset effects on achievement are.

### `sisk-2018`

Sisk, V. F., Burgoyne, A. P., Sun, J., Butler, J. L., & Macnamara, B. N. (2018). To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29505339/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 5 y to 25 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Mindset is only weakly related to academic achievement, and mindset interventions have very small average effects, somewhat larger for academically at-risk students.
- Limits: School-age to adult samples.

### `vasquez-2016`

Vasquez, A. C., Patall, E. A., Fong, C. J., Corrigan, A. S., & Pine, L. (2016). Parent autonomy support, academic achievement, and psychosocial functioning: A meta-analysis of research. Educational Psychology Review. [Link](https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s10648-015-9329-z)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Parents' support for their children's autonomy was related to better achievement, motivation and psychological health.
- Limits: A meta-analysis of correlations, mostly in school-age children.
- Also informs: practical-life.

### `denham-2003`

Denham, S. A., Blair, K. A., DeMulder, E., Levitas, J., Sawyer, K., Auerbach-Major, S., & Queenan, P. (2003). Preschool emotional competence: Pathway to social competence? Child Development. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8624.00533)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 143 preschoolers, emotional expressiveness, emotion regulation and emotion knowledge at ages 3-4 predicted social competence in kindergarten.
- Limits: Correlational.

## Practical life and independence

### `white-2019`

White, E. M., DeBoer, M. D., & Scharf, R. J. (2019). Associations between household chores and childhood self-competency. Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30507727/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 9 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In a national sample of nearly 10,000 children, doing chores more often in kindergarten was associated with higher self-rated competence, prosocial behaviour and math scores in third grade, after controls.
- Limits: Parent-reported chores and correlational. News coverage of a different 2019 longitudinal study reported no link between chores and later self-control; that study was not reviewed.

### `tepper-2022`

Tepper, D. L., Howell, T. J., & Bennett, P. C. (2022). Executive functions and household chores: Does engagement in chores predict children's cognition? Australian Occupational Therapy Journal. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9796572/)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 5 y to 13 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In parent reports on 207 children aged 5-13, doing self-care and family-care chores was related to better working memory and inhibition. Pet-care chores were not.
- Limits: Cross-sectional parent report. Children with better executive function may simply be given more chores.

### `lillard-2017`

Lillard, A. S., Heise, M. J., Richey, E. M., Tong, X., Hart, A., & Bray, P. M. (2017). Montessori preschool elevates and equalizes child outcomes: A longitudinal study. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5670361)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Among 141 children whose places were decided by lottery, those in public Montessori preschools did better over three years on academic achievement, social understanding and mastery orientation than those who lost the lottery.
- Limits: Two schools in one city. It tests a whole program, so the result cannot be attributed to practical-life work specifically.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

## Cooking

### `vanderhorst-2014`

van der Horst, K., Ferrage, A., & Rytz, A. (2014). Involving children in meal preparation. Effects on food intake. Appetite. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24709485/)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 6 y to 10 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: 47 children aged 6-10 who helped a parent cook a meal ate substantially more salad, and more of the meal overall, than children whose parent cooked alone. They also reported feeling more positive.
- Limits: One meal in a research kitchen, with children older than this band. Authors were employed by a food company.

### `hersch-2014`

Hersch, D., Perdue, L., Ambroz, T., & Boucher, J. L. (2014). The impact of cooking classes on food-related preferences, attitudes, and behaviors of school-aged children: A systematic review of the evidence, 2003-2014. Preventing Chronic Disease. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222785)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 5 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Eight studies of cooking programs for children aged 5-12 found positive effects on food preferences, attitudes and eating behaviour.
- Limits: Few studies with weak designs. No evidence here on cooking and academic skills.

## Nature and outdoors

### `he-2015`

He, M., Xiang, F., Zeng, Y., Mai, J., Chen, Q., Zhang, J., et al. (2015). Effect of time spent outdoors at school on the development of myopia among children in China: A randomized clinical trial. JAMA. [Link](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/article-abstract/2441261)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 9 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Adding one 40-minute outdoor class to each school day for three years cut the cumulative incidence of myopia from 39.5% to 30.4% in first-graders.
- Limits: Six- and seven-year-olds in Guangzhou, where myopia is very common. The size of the effect may differ elsewhere.
- Also informs: movement.

### `kuo-2019`

Kuo, M., Barnes, M., & Jordan, C. (2019). Do experiences with nature promote learning? Converging evidence of a cause-and-effect relationship. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00305/pdf)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Argues that time in nature improves attention, stress, self-discipline and engagement with learning, drawing on experimental and correlational studies.
- Limits: A narrative review by advocates. Many of the underlying studies are small or correlational.

### `dankiw-2020`

Dankiw, K. A., Tsiros, M. D., Baldock, K. L., & Kumar, S. (2020). The impacts of unstructured nature play on health in early childhood development: A systematic review. PLoS ONE. [Link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7018039/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Across 16 studies, unstructured play in natural settings was associated with more physical activity and with better cognitive, social and emotional outcomes.
- Limits: Evidence quality rated low, with inconsistent definitions of nature play.

## Building and engineering

### `verdine-2014`

Verdine, B. N., Golinkoff, R. M., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Newcombe, N. S., Filipowicz, A. T., & Chang, A. (2014). Deconstructing building blocks: Preschoolers' spatial assembly performance relates to early mathematical skills. Child Development. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3962809)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 3 y to 3 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 100 three-year-olds, the ability to copy a block construction from a model was related to early math skill. Children from lower-income families were already behind and heard fewer spatial words.
- Limits: Correlational, in three-year-olds.
- Also informs: math.

### `uttal-2013`

Uttal, D. H., Meadow, N. G., Tipton, E., Hand, L. L., Alden, A. R., Warren, C., & Newcombe, N. S. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22663761/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 25 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 217 studies, spatial skills improved with training by nearly half a standard deviation on average. The gains lasted and transferred to spatial tasks that were not trained.
- Limits: All ages, with few preschool studies.

### `hawes-2022`

Hawes, Z. C. K., Gilligan-Lee, K. A., & Mix, K. S. (2022). Effects of spatial training on mathematics performance: A meta-analysis. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35073120/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 29 studies, spatial training improved math performance by roughly a quarter of a standard deviation. Training with physical materials worked better than training without.
- Limits: Effects were larger in older children, and preschool evidence is thin. Moderator details are recalled from memory.
- Also informs: math.

### `levine-2012`

Levine, S. C., Ratliff, K. R., Huttenlocher, J., & Cannon, J. (2012). Early puzzle play: A predictor of preschoolers' spatial transformation skill. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3289766)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 2 y 2 mo to 4 y 6 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Children who were seen playing with puzzles between 26 and 46 months had better spatial transformation skill at 54 months, controlling for parent education, income and overall parent talk.
- Limits: 53 families, correlational.

### `pruden-2011`

Pruden, S. M., Levine, S. C., & Huttenlocher, J. (2011). Children's spatial thinking: Does talk about the spatial world matter? Developmental Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3372906)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 mo to 4 y 6 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: The number of spatial words parents used (shapes, sizes, features such as edge and corner) between 14 and 46 months predicted how many the child used, which predicted spatial task performance at 54 months.
- Limits: Small sample, correlational.

## Second language (optional)

### `kuhl-2003`

Kuhl, P. K., Tsao, F.-M., & Liu, H.-M. (2003). Foreign-language experience in infancy: Effects of short-term exposure and social interaction on phonetic learning. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC166444)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 9 mo to 10 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Nine-month-olds learned Mandarin speech-sound contrasts from 12 live sessions with a speaker, but not from the same material on video or audio.
- Limits: Infants and speech-sound learning only.

### `hartshorne-2018`

Hartshorne, J. K., Tenenbaum, J. B., & Pinker, S. (2018). A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers. Cognition. [Link](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/126641)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 0 mo to 70 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 670,000 people, the ability to learn grammar stayed high until about age 17, but reaching a native-like level required starting by about age 10-12.
- Limits: An online English grammar quiz with a self-selected sample.

### `byers-2013`

Byers-Heinlein, K., & Lew-Williams, C. (2013). Bilingualism in the early years: What the science says. LEARNing Landscapes. [Link](https://learninglandscapes.ca/index.php/learnland/article/view/632)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 0 mo to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children are not confused by hearing two languages. How well each language is learned depends on the amount and quality of exposure to it, and no single family strategy is best.
- Limits: A review written for parents and practitioners.

### `lehtonen-2018`

Lehtonen, M., Soveri, A., Laine, A., Jarvenpaa, J., de Bruin, A., & Antfolk, J. (2018). Is bilingualism associated with enhanced executive functioning in adults? A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/157474/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 18 y to 80 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 152 studies of adults, there was no bilingual advantage in executive function once publication bias was corrected.
- Limits: Adults only.

### `gunnerud-2020`

Gunnerud, H. L., ten Braak, D., Reikeras, E. K. L., Donolato, E., & Melby-Lervag, M. (2020). Is bilingualism related to a cognitive advantage in children? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://uv.uio.no/isp/forskning/publikasjoner/nye-publikasjoner/gunnerud-ten-braak-reikeras-donolato---melby-lerva.html)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In children, the overall bilingual advantage in executive function was very small and not robust, appearing mainly in particular subgroups.
- Limits: Summary recalled from memory; the paper was not re-read on the check date.
